The waterflea Disparalona rostrata is a small-bodied chydorid cladoceran inhabiting the littoral zones of temperate freshwater systems. At the moment of birth, neonates measure approximately 0.034 cm [Lb = approximately 0.034 cm] in total length, a modest size that reflects the limited yolk reserves available during embryonic development. This initial length is notably smaller than that of many co-occurring daphniids, likely due to the species' selective filter-feeding on fine particulate organic matter. Newborn individuals resemble miniature versions of the adults and begin filtering within hours following their release from the brood chamber. The early juvenile phase is characterized by rapid linear growth, as individuals must quickly attain a size refuge from small invertebrate predators such as cyclopoid copepods and early instars of Chaoborus larvae. Measurements obtained from laboratory-reared cohorts indicate that the carapace elongates steadily during the first several instars, with ecdysis occurring every two to three days under optimal food concentrations. The total length at birth (0.034 cm) [Lb = 0.034 cm] provides a critical baseline for constructing growth curves that differentiate this taxon from morphologically similar congeners.

Upon reaching sexual maturity, individuals of Disparalona rostrata attain a distinct size threshold that marks the onset of reproductive capability. The total length at puberty has been recorded at 0.048 cm [Lp = 0.048 cm], a value that aligns closely with the size at which the first instar bearing differentiated gonads appears in dissected specimens. This milestone typically coincides with the completion of approximately five to six juvenile instars, depending on local thermal regimes and food availability. The transition to adulthood is accompanied by a reorganisation of resource use, with ingested carbon increasingly directed toward vitellogenesis rather than further linear expansion. In field populations, individuals at this length are readily identifiable by the presence of a fully developed postabdomen and a functional set of thoracic appendages specialized for filtration. The value of 0.048 cm [Lp = 0.048 cm] represents a reliable indicator of the pubertal threshold, and it is frequently employed in life-table analyses to distinguish the pre-reproductive from the reproductively active segment of the population.

The maximum body size reached during the lifetime of Disparalona rostrata is an important determinant of competitive ability and fecundity. The ultimate total length attains 0.0572 cm [Li = 0.0572 cm], a value derived from repeated measurements of senescent individuals in laboratory cultures maintained until natural death. This asymptotic length constrains the volume of the brood chamber and thus sets an upper bound on clutch size, as larger females can accommodate more developing embryos simultaneously. Comparative studies of chydorid body size suggest that 0.0572 cm [Li = 0.0572 cm] is near the upper range for the genus Disparalona, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes early maturation over continued somatic expansion. The dry mass corresponding to this terminal body size has been estimated at 1.2 micrograms  through allometric scaling relationships established for closely related species, providing a useful metric for quantifying individual biomass within community-level energetic models.

At a constant water temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], females produce two eggs per moult interval [N_R_i = two eggs per moult interval], with each moult occurring over an average period of 7.3 days. This yields an annual moult frequency of approximately 50 moults per year [F_R_i = approximately 50 moults per year], meaning that females deposit eggs at regular intervals throughout their reproductive lifespan under those thermal conditions. The temperature of 14 °C reflects typical spring or autumn water temperatures in the shallow littoral habitats this species occupies, periods when phytoplankton concentrations are elevated. Under these conditions, the combination of clutch size and moult frequency yields a steady supply of neonates that sustains population abundance through the growing season.

At 19 °C [T = 19 °C], a temperature representative of summer epilimnetic conditions in many eutrophic ponds, the time since birth at puberty has been observed to be 8 days [tp = 8 days]. This short pre-reproductive interval allows the species to complete multiple generations within a single warm season, contributing to its ability to colonize ephemeral habitats. The higher thermal regime accelerates the moulting cycle by reducing the intermoult duration, thereby shortening the interval between birth and the pubertal moult. Comparisons with other chydorid taxa indicate that an 8-day pre-reproductive phase since birth (8 days since birth) [tp = 8 days since birth] is relatively brief, consistent with a life history that balances quick generation turnover against moderate investment per offspring at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C].
